reference.source: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in HSD11B2, encoding 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2
This enzyme normally converts cortisol to inactive cortisone within mineralocorticoid target cells, protecting the mineralocorticoid receptor from being activated by cortisol
When it fails, cortisol floods and activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing a mineralocorticoid-excess state despite normal aldosterone
The hallmark is severe low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and both renin and aldosterone are suppressed
An elevated urinary cortisol-to-cortisone metabolite ratio is characteristic and helps confirm the diagnosis
The acquired phenocopy is heavy licorice or carbenoxolone ingestion, which inhibits the same enzyme
Management combines mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade and sometimes an ENaC blocker with salt restriction; suppressing endogenous cortisol may be considered in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess arises from deficiency of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, an enzyme expressed in aldosterone-responsive tissues that inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone, but is normally circulating at far higher concentrations; the enzyme provides tissue specificity by locally clearing cortisol so that only aldosterone reaches the receptor. When the enzyme is deficient, intracellular cortisol accumulates and inappropriately activates the mineralocorticoid receptor in the distal nephron, driving sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen loss. The resulting volume expansion causes low-renin hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis, while the same volume expansion suppresses aldosterone, so the biochemistry shows mineralocorticoid effects without a raised mineralocorticoid hormone.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with mineralocorticoid excess (11-beta or 17-alpha hydroxylase types)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed)
Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis
Urinary steroid metabolite profile showing an increased cortisol-to-cortisone ratio
Screening for licorice, carbenoxolone and other enzyme-inhibiting exposures
Renal and cardiac end-organ assessment given severe hypertension
redFlags: Severe hypertension presenting in childhood or young adulthood
Profound hypokalaemia with weakness or arrhythmia
Hypertensive end-organ damage including nephrocalcinosis and left ventricular hypertrophy
Failure to thrive or growth restriction in affected children
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on how early treatment begins; poorly controlled disease leads to severe hypertensive complications and chronic kidney damage, whereas mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade with salt restriction can achieve reasonable control.
pitfalls: Attributing the picture to primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone
Missing a dietary licorice or carbenoxolone cause of an identical biochemical picture
Relying on aldosterone antagonism alone when severe disease may also need ENaC blockade and salt restriction
Overlooking the recessive inheritance and the need to evaluate siblings
references: Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
